strengths: Training-free and efficient pipeline: By removing per-scene iterative contrastive learning and latent feature optimization, the method dramatically simplifies the pipeline and eliminates per-scene feature training overhead and multi-gigabyte feature storage requirements.

Effective resolution of multi-view visual inconsistency: Leveraging a multimodal LLM/VLM to summarize multi-view observations into descriptive textual candidate names elegantly circumvents the severe view-dependent noise and semantic drift inherent to averaging CLIP image embeddings.

Principled boundary refinement: The neutral point identification mechanism, which combines multi-view semantic entropy with Gaussian opacity filtering, effectively purifies ambiguous boundary points and improves segmentation sharpness.

Strong empirical performance: Across both 3D object selection on LERF and 3D semantic segmentation on ScanNet, MUSplat achieves clear gains over state-of-the-art point-based (e.g., OpenGaussian, InstanceGaussian, Dr.Splat) and pixel-based baselines.

Clear ablation experiments: The ablation studies in Section 4.3 cleanly isolate and validate the individual utility of both stages of neutral point processing as well as the VLM-based textual feature distillation compared to various CLIP image aggregation baselines.
weaknesses: Omission of end-to-end preprocessing time: While Table 1 lists 'Train Time' as 'None' for MUSplat, the end-to-end pipeline requires running SAM at three granularity levels, DAM2SAM tracking over all frames, 3D mask back-projection, and querying Gemini 2.5 Pro. A comprehensive wall-clock time comparison including all data preparation and inference steps against baseline training/inference times is necessary for a fair evaluation of efficiency.

Dependence on proprietary external VLMs: The method relies on Gemini 2.5 Pro via an external API. The submission would be significantly strengthened by evaluating whether open-source, locally hosted VLMs (e.g., LLaVA, InternVL, Qwen2-VL) yield comparable performance, as well as reporting the monetary and latency costs per scene.

Insufficient evaluation of polysemy: While 'polysemy' is prominently featured in the title and introduction as a key limitation of prior art, the paper primarily tests standard single-label retrieval/segmentation benchmarks (LERF and ScanNet). A targeted qualitative or quantitative experiment explicitly demonstrating multi-concept querying (e.g., querying an object simultaneously by material, function, and taxonomic category) would more convincingly validate this claim.

Sensitivity to hyperparameters: The framework introduces several heuristic thresholds (entropy threshold $\tau_h$, opacity threshold $\tau_\alpha$, VLM view count $N$, and similarity threshold $\eta$). An analysis exploring the sensitivity of the performance to variations in these thresholds is missing.

strengths: Practical and efficient training-free paradigm: By eliminating expensive per-scene semantic feature optimization and codebook training, MUSplat dramatically reduces feature storage (from ~3GB to ~3MB) and GPU memory consumption while remaining plug-and-play.

Strong quantitative performance: The proposed method demonstrates impressive results, surpassing prior point-based and pixel-based 3DGS baselines on both the LERF benchmark (54.3 mIoU vs. 43.6 mIoU for Dr.Splat) and ScanNet 3D semantic segmentation.

Effective multi-view grounding via VLM distillation: Using a VLM to generate canonical textual hypotheses from key views effectively circumvents the well-known view-inconsistency and domain-shift issues of 2D CLIP visual embeddings, as shown in the ablation study.

Well-motivated neutral point refinement: Formulating boundary point uncertainty using multi-view semantic entropy combined with geometric opacity filtering provides a neat, principled mechanism to clean up ambiguous boundary Gaussians without retraining.
weaknesses: Vague end-to-end preprocessing runtime: While the paper highlights 'Train Time: None' and states adaptation takes 'mere minutes', the full data preparation and tracking pipeline (multi-granularity SAM + DAM2SAM tracking over all views + VLM queries per object) constitutes non-trivial computation. The manuscript should report total end-to-end wall-clock time from raw images/3DGS to queryable representation.

Under-evaluated polysemy claim: Although 'Polysemous' is featured prominently in the title and introduction, the empirical evaluation only tests standard open-vocabulary benchmarks (single-query retrieval on LERF and class-label segmentation on ScanNet). A dedicated experiment explicitly testing multi-attribute/multi-concept retrieval on the same instance (e.g., material vs. category vs. functional affordance) is needed to validate this claim.

Reliance on proprietary VLM without open-source comparison: The instance feature extraction relies on Gemini 2.5 Pro via an API. The paper lacks ablation or sensitivity analysis comparing performance against open-source VLMs (e.g., Qwen2-VL, InternVL, or LLaVA), leaving the framework's reproducibility and robustness across different language backbones unclear.

Lack of hyperparameter sensitivity analysis: The pipeline introduces several heuristic thresholds (entropy threshold tau_h, opacity threshold tau_alpha, matching threshold eta, and top-N views), but no ablations or robustness curves are provided to show how sensitive the framework is to these selections.

strengths: The paper addresses a critical and practical limitation of existing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) semantic understanding methods: the reliance on computationally demanding per-scene feature training, offering an entirely training-free alternative.

The proposed object-level grouping strategy is technically sound; combining transmittance-weighted mask back-projection with entropy- and opacity-based neutral point refinement effectively resolves boundary ambiguities without extra neural network optimization.

The VLM-based textual distillation mechanism provides an elegant solution to the cross-view visual inconsistency and feature collapse common in CLIP image embeddings, generating stable, canonical textual hypotheses for instance matching.

Empirical performance is strong across standard benchmarks: MUSplat achieves state-of-the-art results on LERF (54.3 mIoU vs. 43.6 for Dr.Splat and 40.7 for InstanceGaussian) and ScanNet semantic segmentation, while reducing semantic feature storage from ~3GB to ~3MB and requiring lower peak VRAM.
weaknesses: Mismatch between the polysemy claim and experimental evaluation: While polysemy is highlighted in the paper's title and introduction as a primary motivator, the experiments primarily evaluate standard single-target open-vocabulary selection and semantic segmentation benchmarks (LERF and ScanNet). There is no explicit benchmark, quantitative evaluation, or dedicated qualitative suite assessing multi-concept/polysemous retrieval.

Heavy reliance on a closed-source proprietary VLM (Gemini 2.5 Pro): The paper claims the method is VLM-agnostic, but no ablation or comparison is provided using open-source VLMs (e.g., LLaVA, InternVL, or Qwen2-VL). This leaves open questions regarding how much the performance gain depends on the reasoning capability of a frontier commercial model.

Incomplete accounting of preprocessing wall-clock runtime: Table 1 highlights 'Train Time: None', which is true for semantic field optimization, but the cumulative time required for SAM segmentation at multiple granularities, multi-view tracking via DAM2SAM, periodic re-detection, and VLM API calls is not reported. A comprehensive end-to-end runtime breakdown is necessary for a fair efficiency comparison with baseline training pipelines.

Missing implementation details: Key hyperparameter choices (such as thresholds tau_h, tau_alpha, matching threshold eta, and selected key view count N) as well as the exact prompt template provided to the VLM are omitted from the main text.

strengths: Compelling conceptual motivation: Decoupling geometric representation from high-dimensional semantic feature fields through an extrinsic index layer effectively tackles semantic bloat (reducing feature storage from gigabytes to megabytes) and avoids expensive contrastive optimization.

Well-designed neutral point filtering mechanism: Identifying ambiguous boundary Gaussians via multi-view label entropy and filtering them via opacity effectively improves boundary delineation without corrupting underlying rendering geometry.

Substantial practical efficiency: The framework is training-free, operates within ~9 minutes on complex scenes, requires significantly less VRAM (~8 GB), and eliminates the need for per-scene semantic feature learning.

Thorough evaluation and insightful ablations: The manuscript provides extensive comparisons on LERF and ScanNet, accompanied by detailed ablations regarding mask sparsity, threshold sensitivity, prompt quantity, and VLM backbones, along with downstream applications like 3D object editing.
weaknesses: Unfair baseline advantage through advanced VLM reasoning: The method leverages Gemini 2.5 Pro to interpret masked views into descriptive text hypotheses, whereas baseline approaches primarily rely on standard CLIP/DINO feature pooling. The ablation in Table 6 indicates a notable performance drop (from 54.3 to 47.0 mIoU) when using weaker models, making it difficult to fully isolate whether the gains stem from the extrinsic grouping paradigm or the superior reasoning capacity of the VLM.

Gap to top training-based / 2D methods on LERF: While ExtrinSplat achieves state-of-the-art among training-free 3D methods, its overall LERF mIoU (54.3) remains behind top-performing training-based methods such as LAGA (64.0) and 2D methods like 3DVLGS (62.0). A deeper discussion clarifying this performance trade-off would strengthen the paper.

Dependence on upstream multi-view mask association: The quality of grouping and subsequent VLM prompting relies heavily on the tracking fidelity of DAM2SAM and initial SAM masks. As noted in the failure analysis, severe tracking drift or occlusion across frames can result in fragmented 3D groups or erroneous VLM descriptions.

strengths: Clear and compelling motivation: The manuscript identifies key pain points in existing open-vocabulary 3DGS methods—specifically feature bloat (gigabytes of per-point embeddings), semantic rigidity (difficulty handling hierarchical polysemy), and boundary ambiguity caused by transitional/blending Gaussians.

Efficient decoupled paradigm: Replacing dense per-Gaussian feature fields with an extrinsic index layer that pairs point-index groupings with lightweight text embeddings reduces feature storage by roughly three orders of magnitude (~3GB to ~3MB) while requiring zero scene-specific network training.

Principled handling of boundary artifacts ('neutral points'): Formulating neutral points via multi-view label entropy and opacity filtering provides an intuitive, training-free mechanism to clean up transitional boundary splats without harming geometry.

Solid empirical evaluation and ablation study: The method demonstrates strong performance on both LERF and ScanNet benchmarks, outperforming prior training-free 3D baselines. The paper provides insightful analyses, including the impact of VLM choice, prompt counts, mask sparsity, and run-time breakdowns.
weaknesses: Clarity on baseline comparisons: In Section 4.1 (Tab. 2), the paper claims a new SOTA outperforming previous methods by 3.9 mIoU. However, this holds specifically against 3D training-free baselines (LUDVIG at 50.4 vs. Ours at 54.3), whereas training-based methods (e.g., LAGA at 64.0) and 2D methods (3DVLGS at 62.0) achieve higher numbers. The scope of this comparison should be stated more precisely in the text.

Reliance on heavyweight external VLMs: The performance relies heavily on high-capacity VLMs (Gemini 2.5 Pro yields 54.3 mIoU vs. SenseNova at 47.0). While using text distillation is an effective design choice, relying on commercial proprietary APIs introduces external cost, latency, and potential reproducibility challenges.

Limited novelty in individual algorithmic components: The framework combines established components (SAM prompting, DAM2SAM tracking, transmittance-based mask back-projection, VLM-prompted instance captioning, and CLIP text matching). The primary contribution lies in the system-level integration and the extrinsic decoupled formulation rather than new core algorithms.

strengths: Compelling paradigm shift with substantial storage and memory reduction: By decoupling semantics from 3D Gaussians into an extrinsic index layer linking object groups to textual hypotheses, the framework achieves an impressive ~1000x reduction in feature storage (~3MB vs ~3GB) and eliminates expensive per-scene neural feature optimization.

Well-motivated handling of boundary 'neutral points': Formulating object boundary Gaussians as semantically neutral via a two-stage filter (multi-view semantic entropy and opacity) offers an intuitive, computationally lightweight (0.1% overhead) solution to boundary ambiguity in 3DGS.

Comprehensive empirical analysis and ablation: The paper includes extensive qualitative and quantitative evaluations on LERF and ScanNet, accompanied by detailed component-level ablations (filtering thresholds, prompt count, VLM choice, sparse mask inputs, and computational runtime breakdown).
weaknesses: Unfair baseline comparison due to external VLM capacity: ExtrinSplat relies on Gemini 2.5 Pro to interpret multi-view crops and generate canonical text hypotheses, whereas baseline approaches typically operate strictly with CLIP (ViT-B/L) visual encoders. Table 6 indicates that when using other models (e.g., SenseNova 6.5 Pro), performance drops from 54.3 to 47.0 mIoU (falling behind training-free baselines like LUDVIG at 50.4), suggesting a substantial portion of the gains stems from the reasoning power of the proprietary VLM rather than the 3D grouping representation.

Modular combination of off-the-shelf components: The framework largely chains together existing foundation tools (SAM, DAM2SAM, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and CLIP) with standard volumetric back-projection heuristics. While engineering-effective, the core technical contribution on the 3D vision side is relatively incremental.

Performance gaps compared to top methods: On the LERF object selection benchmark (Table 2), ExtrinSplat (54.3 mIoU) remains noticeably behind existing 3D training-based methods such as LAGA (64.0 mIoU) and pixel-based 2D methods like 3DVLGS (62.0 mIoU) and Occam's LGS (61.3 mIoU). A more nuanced discussion regarding the trade-offs between precision and training-free deployment is warranted.

Unverified claims on polysemy and hierarchy: Although the paper repeatedly emphasizes multi-granularity and semantic polysemy (e.g., part vs. object) as a core motivation for the extrinsic paradigm, neither LERF nor ScanNet benchmarks explicitly evaluate hierarchical part-to-whole retrieval or disambiguation against baselines.
